questions.question: Why is the sound-alike medication flag placed inline after the drug name rather than in the right-hand margin?

seeded.answer:
[1] Participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag in the right-hand margin. 5:1 preference for inline placement.
[2] The flag is placed inline, immediately after the medication name, because participants preferred it over a right-hand margin badge.
[3] Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: In a 6-person concept test, a distinct sound-alike-medication flag was recognized as different from generic confidence highlighting. The GA-candidate round treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. Any rollout needs to actively counter that over-trust framing, not just ship the flag.

sources.title: Interview — Family Physician on the Plan Section and Medication Changes at Sign-Off
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe sessions tested medication accuracy in drafts: dosage errors in v0.1 and v0.2, sound-alike drug names at the GA release candidate, and a concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag (2026-02-10). The plan section has so far come up only from the reader's side: a care coordinator goes straight to the plan and the medication list in the visit notes they read before an outreach call (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31, :43), and the 2026-03-17 clinic nurse interview (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes) heard that plan items sometimes land in the body of the note rather than the plan (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes/session-notes.md:30). None of those sessions asked the person who signs the draft how they check the plan section, where decisions made during the visit, including medication changes, are supposed to end up. This session asked a family physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, how they check the plan and the medication lines in a draft before they sign.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a family medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician enters orders, including medication orders, separately. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. The distinct sound-alike medication flag tested on 2026-02-10 has not shipped; there is no distinct medication marking beyond the confidence underline. They did not take part in any earlier session. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (plan section) When a decision is talked through over several minutes, the draft sometimes puts the reasoning in the assessment and only part of the decision in the plan, or leaves a follow-up interval in the body of the note. Before signing they read the plan against what they remember deciding and move or add items by hand. They put it at "a couple of times on a full clinic day", an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (medication changes) They enter medication orders themselves, so they know what they decided; the question at sign-off is whether the note says the same thing. Their main check is that every medication change in the plan matches the order they placed, and that it is written as a decision. When the draft words a change tentatively, as it was discussed rather than as it was decided, they rewrite it. They said they make this check on every medication line, underlined or not.
[MEDIUM] (sound-alike names) They recalled one sound-alike drug name since GA, glyburide written where glipizide had been said, and said it was underlined. It is one recollection, not a rate; the GA release-candidate round records sound-alike names as a known, monitored error type (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:31). They said they would check medication lines against the order whether or not anything marked them, because a wrong name can be heard confidently.
Representative Quotes
"I put the order in myself, so I know what I decided. The question is whether the note says the same thing." — Physician (Family Medicine), P147
"'We talked about lowering the dose' isn't a plan. I change it to what we actually did." — Physician (Family Medicine), P147
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that decisions made during the visit, especially medication changes and follow-up intervals, need to reach the plan section, worded as decisions.
When drafts are evaluated, check the plan section's completeness against what was decided in the visit, not only transcription accuracy.
When the distinct medication flag's design is next reviewed, note that this physician checks every medication line against the order regardless of marking; whether a flag would change that is untested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often plan items land outside the plan section is not measured; "a couple of times on a full clinic day" is one physician's impression.
Whether NPs and PAs, or other physicians, check the plan and medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag would change how signers check medication lines is untested; it has not shipped.

sources.title: Interview — Infusion Nurse on Medication Changes in Scribe-Drafted Notes
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The medication thread in ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinements.md rests on a concept test of a distinct sound-alike medication flag with the people who review and sign scribe drafts: physicians and NPs (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/participants.md). Nobody who reads a signed, scribe-drafted note and then gives the medication has been asked about it. This session asked an infusion nurse how they check medication changes in the treating provider's visit note before they administer, and what, if anything, they see on medication lines in a signed note.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a registered nurse in an ambulatory infusion clinic, mid-career. Patients come in for scheduled infusions, and before starting one the nurse checks the infusion order against the treating provider's most recent visit note, which since the January 2026 GA is often scribe-drafted. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs only; the participant doesn't use it, and their own charting is manual. They did not take part in any earlier session. They are not P138, the primary care clinic nurse interviewed in March 2026, and they don't do care coordination or post-discharge calls. The distinct medication flag is recorded in the corpus as a concept test (2026-02-10) and a wireframe in review ( wireframes/ambient-scribe-medication-flag.md ), whose hover copy reads "verify before signing"; nothing was shown in this session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (checking before administering) Before every infusion they compare the order with the treating provider's latest visit note, looking for a medication change: a changed dose, a held infusion, a premedication added or stopped, or a lab value that has to be checked first. They give the medication from the order, not the note; the note is how they find out whether the order still reflects what was decided at the visit. When the two disagree, they hold the infusion and contact the provider before starting. In scribe-drafted notes they sometimes find a change in the body of the note, written up from the conversation, rather than in the plan, or worded so that they can't tell whether it was decided ("we'll probably bring the dose down"). They recalled holding an infusion to check for this reason "maybe once or twice a month" since GA; that is an informal recollection, not a count, and they couldn't say how many of those came from the scribe's drafting and how many from the provider. This is the same pattern of plan items landing in the body that the March 2026 clinic nurse described (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes/session-notes.md:30), in a different setting: here the cost is a delayed infusion before administration, not a delayed callback.
[MEDIUM] (the flag and readers) The medication flag has so far been designed and tested for the person signing the note. This nurse reads the note after it is signed and acts on its medication lines. In the signed notes they read, they said they have not seen any marking on medication lines, neither a flag nor an underline; that is what they see, not a statement of how the product behaves. Their working assumption is that every medication line in a signed note was checked by the provider. That is a reader's version of the over-trust risk the concept test found in 2 of 6 signers, who trusted unflagged lines more: a reader who never sees a flag treats every signed line as checked. They said that if a line had been flagged and the provider then confirmed or changed it, they would want to know, because that is the line they would check against the order first. That is an expectation; no such view exists. This extends the medication-flag finding to readers who didn't write the note.
Representative Quotes
"I don't hang anything off the note, I hang it off the order. The note is how I find out if the order's still right." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
"If it's signed, I assume they checked the meds. I've never seen anything on a med line that tells me different." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that medication changes decided at the visit need to reach the plan section as decided changes, because infusion nurses check them against the order before administering.
When the medication flag's design is next reviewed, include nurses who read signed notes and give the medication as a user group, and decide explicitly whether anything about a flag, and what the signer did with it, should reach them. Don't assume either answer.
Keep this evidence separate from the care coordination evidence on after-visit summaries: this is the visit note checked against the order before administration, not the summary a patient takes home.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Whether the medication flag, or any confidence marking, stays visible after a note is signed is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here. This nurse has not seen any marking on signed notes, which says what they see, not how the product behaves; and the corpus records the distinct flag only as a concept test and a wireframe in review.
How often an infusion is held because the note and the order disagree is not measured; "once or twice a month" is one nurse's recollection, and how many of those trace back to scribe drafting is not known.
Whether other infusion nurses, or nurses in other clinics, check the note against the order the same way is not known; this is one interview.
How often the after-visit summary misses medication changes remains open in the care coordination evidence; it was not discussed here.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

sources.title: Interview — IT Administrator on Schedule Access and Staff Invites
sources.excerpt:
Objective
In the 2026-02-03 usability test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at Connect calendar because they did not think they could approve Compass AI's access to patient appointments, and both IT Administrators asked which fields are read before connecting ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:51-52 ). This session asked one IT Administrator who approves access requests across practices what has to happen before a new system can read a practice's appointment schedule, and who can start that. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training (in 2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:62 , "onboarding" means training copy for clinicians).
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an IT Administrator who handles access requests for systems used across Meridian's practices. They had not used the Compass AI practice setup flow. The researcher described steps 3 (Connect calendar) and 4 (Invite your team) as the 2026-02-03 build shows them, and what the step 3 screen does and doesn't say, without sharing what other participants said. The participant did not name the scheduling system that holds the appointment schedule, and these notes don't record which system it is. This is their account of the approval process, not a review of its records.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (schedule access: privacy review) In their account, any new system that reads the appointment schedule needs a privacy review request before it is connected, and a Practice Administrator can't start one: requests are filed by IT. A practice that wants the calendar connected has to ask IT to file the request. They didn't know whether one had been filed for Compass AI.
[MEDIUM] (schedule access: still PHI) They described scheduling as the lowest-risk data on the CMIO's PHI ordering, but still PHI: the schedule carries patient names and, depending on the fields read, visit reasons. They saw this as consistent with the ordering, not a contradiction of it, because the ordering ranks the risk and doesn't remove the review.
Representative Quotes
"Lowest risk isn't no risk. It's still patient names on a schedule. It still goes through privacy review, it just shouldn't take long." — IT Administrator, P160
"A practice admin can't put in that request. They call us, we file it. If the screen just asks them to click connect, it's asking the wrong person." — IT Administrator, P160
Recommendations
On Connect calendar, route an administrator who can't approve schedule access to IT, consistent with the "Send to IT for approval" path recommended on 2026-02-03 ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:75-76 ).
Before more practices set up, confirm with IT whether a privacy review request for Compass AI reading the appointment schedule has been filed, and list the fields it covers.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Has a privacy review request for Compass AI's schedule access been filed, and which fields does it cover?
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through the setup flow's invites, or both? The participant didn't know.

questions.question: Why does the session lock recovery flow add a paused state instead of changing the idle timeout?

questions.question: Why does the confidence-highlighted draft review leave high-confidence lines unmarked?

seeded.answer: The confidence-highlighted draft review leaves high-confidence lines unmarked "to invite skimming" [1].

sources.title: Confidence-Highlighted Draft Review — Hi-Fi Mockup (GA Candidate)
sources.excerpt: Two-state treatment. The 2026-01-13 session notes record only that low-confidence transcription was shown in a subtle underline ( :30 ). The rest is the designer's spec and wasn't recorded in the test: high-confidence lines render as default text with no marking (deliberately inviting skimming), low-confidence lines also get an on-hover explanation, and there is no separate medium-confidence tier. Deliberately avoids color-only signaling, per the cross-cutting accessibility finding — flagged lines are distinguishable by the underline itself, not color alone.
